title: Overture
one_line_summary: A jargon-setting prelude that moves from the Newtonian principle of relativity and Einstein's light-speed postulate to light cones, flat versus curved spacetime, the metric as a field and a word-equation form of Einstein's equation, then refreshes Newtonian gravity (field, potential, Gauss's law, Poisson's equation, escape speed, Mercury) as the weak-field baseline, and closes with the reader profile, a map of the six Parts and the rules for geometrized units.
role_in_book: Chapter 0 is the orientation layer for the whole book. It names the vocabulary that Part I (special relativity, vectors, the metric) and Part II (curvature, the field equation) will make precise: inertial frames, boosts, covariance, light cones, events, line elements, curvature as non-parallelism, and the metric field. It also fixes the Newtonian results (g = -grad Phi, Poisson's equation, Phi/c^2 as a strength gauge) that Chapter 6 and Chapter 13 use when demanding that general relativity reduce to Newton in the weak-field limit, and it sets up the unit conventions (c = 1 from Chapter 2, G = c = 1 from Part III) that every later chapter relies on. Nothing here is derived relativistically; its job is motivation, a shared dictionary, and a Newtonian launch pad.

assumed_background.topic: Newton's laws of motion and circular-orbit dynamics (centripetal force)
Newton's inverse-square law of gravitation and gravitational potential energy
Vector calculus: gradient, divergence, surface and volume integrals, divergence theorem
Electrostatics: Coulomb field, Gauss's law, Poisson's equation (used as an analogy)
Basic astronomical facts: Earth-Moon-Sun geometry, planetary orbits, stars
Euclidean geometry, including the parallel postulate
Awareness that quantum mechanics exists (for remarks on classical field theory and neutron stars)

learning_objectives: Reader can state the principle of relativity and explain why it rules out an absolute rest frame in Newtonian physics.
Reader can define an inertial frame and a boost, and classify rotations, translations, reflections and boosts as symmetry transformations.
Reader can state Einstein's second postulate (invariance of light speed) and explain why the resulting theory is called 'special'.
Reader can explain what it means for a theory to be covariant, and why special relativity requires Lorentz (not Galilean) boosts.
Reader can sketch a light cone on a spacetime diagram and identify which events can influence, or be influenced by, an observer.
Reader can contrast flat spacetime (all light cones aligned) with curved spacetime (cones that cannot all be aligned) at a picture level.
Reader can describe the metric as a field that returns, at each event, the rule for computing intervals between neighbouring events.
Reader can explain how non-parallelism of initially parallel lines (or relative drift of nearby free test particles) diagnoses curvature.
Reader can write the Einstein equation schematically as geometry on one side and matter-energy on the other.
Reader can state the point-mass field g = -GM r_hat/r^2 and potential Phi = -GM/r, and derive Gauss's law for gravity and Poisson's equation using the divergence theorem and a Dirac delta source.
Reader can use surface gravity, orbital period and the Cavendish value of G to estimate the masses and mean densities of the Earth and Sun.
Reader can derive the Newtonian escape speed and find the radius at which it equals c, for a given density or mass.
Reader can use |Phi|/c^2 as an order-of-magnitude gauge of how relativistic a gravitational field is, and cite GPS and Mercury as cases where small effects still matter.
Reader can convert any quantity between SI and geometrized (G = c = 1) units using the factor c^m (G/c^2)^p, and restore constants in G = 8 pi T.

teaching_approach.summary: An informal, question-titled survey ('What is relativity?', 'What is a metric?') that front-loads vocabulary with everyday pictures (a juggler, trains in a station, parade soldiers) and postpones every relativistic derivation. The only real calculations are Newtonian: the authors deliberately rebuild the vector-field, potential and Gauss/Poisson description of gravity, plus back-of-envelope astronomy, so that the reader has a concrete weak-field target and a sense of scale before curvature arrives. Formal Example boxes are used as mini-stories rather than exercises, and margin notes carry biographies, cautions and pointers to later chapters. Example boxes can be long: Example 0.3 grows from weighing the Earth into weighing the Sun and a Newtonian dark-star estimate before it closes.
narrative_arc: Hook: general relativity underlies cosmology, black holes and gravitational waves, yet rests on simple principles.
Relativity before Einstein: inertial frames and the principle of relativity as a symmetry; juggling and train examples.
Add the invariant light speed postulate; explain 'special', covariance and Lorentz covariance.
Picture causality with light cones; a lattice of aligned cones means flat spacetime, disordered cones hint at curvature.
Motivating puzzle: Newton described gravity but gave no mechanism; Einstein's answer is spacetime curvature sourced by matter.
Define a field as a position-to-amplitude machine, single out the metric field, and write Einstein's equation as curvature = matter energy.
Explain the metric via events and line elements; use Euclid's parallel postulate to define curvature operationally.
Reset the Newtonian baseline: force, field, potential, Cavendish, masses and densities of Earth and Sun, dark-star escape speed.
Formalize Newton with flux, divergence theorem, delta functions, Gauss's law and Poisson's equation.
Signal where Newton fails: |Phi| comparable to c^2, yet GPS and Mercury show measurable effects far below that.
Meta-level: reader profile, map of Parts I-VI, advice to read at least 13 chapters, skip-boxes.
Practical tooling: geometrized units, general conversion rule and table, restoring constants in the field equation.
signature_moves: Section titles phrased as naive questions a newcomer would ask, each answered in a page or two.
Principles set off in shaded boxes (principle of relativity, invariant light speed) and Wheeler's slogan in its own box.
Four-case juggler ladder (at rest, constant velocity, constant acceleration, jolting) that previews both special relativity and the equivalence principle in one example.
Visual shorthand for curvature: arrays of light cones that are neatly aligned versus tipped every which way.
Word equation with bracketed phrases instead of symbols for Einstein's equation, deferring tensors.
Newtonian gravity rewritten in field language (vector field, scalar potential, flux, Poisson) as a bridge to a field theory of gravity.
Order-of-magnitude astronomy with modern numbers (weighing the Earth, the Sun's density, the dark-star radius) to build scale intuition.
Dimensionless ratio |Phi|/c^2 introduced as the natural gauge of relativistic gravity, immediately undercut by Mercury and GPS examples.
A single algebraic rule c^m (G/c^2)^p plus a table for unit conversion, demonstrated on the Einstein equation.

sections.title: Chapter opening
sections.summary: Opens with a Carlyle epigraph praising Newtonian gravity as complete, lists what general relativity explains (cosmic structure, black holes, light bending, gravitational waves, cosmic origins), credits Einstein, and promises that despite its reputation the theory rests on easy-to-grasp principles; this chapter will map the route and supply jargon.
key_moves: Set an ironic frame: the epigraph's confidence in Newton is paid off later by the Mercury anomaly.
Reassure: difficulty is mathematical, principles are simple.

sections.title: What is relativity?
sections.summary: Defines inertial frames through Newton's first law, states the principle of relativity and concludes there is no absolute rest frame. Example 0.1 uses a juggler to show that Newtonian reasoning works on a stationary floor, on a uniformly moving train, and even under steady acceleration (which mimics extra gravity), but not under jerky acceleration. The principle is recast as a symmetry under rotations, translations and boosts; Example 0.2 uses the illusion of motion between adjacent trains. Einstein's 1905 invariant light-speed postulate is added, explaining the name 'special' relativity, the idea of covariance and Lorentz covariance. Light cones on spacetime diagrams encode causality; an aligned lattice of cones characterizes flat spacetime.
key_moves: Inertial frame defined operationally: the frames where the first law holds.
No preferred rest frame follows from the principle of relativity.
Juggler ladder distinguishes uniform motion, uniform acceleration (equivalent to a gravitational field) and time-varying acceleration.
Relativity reframed as invariance of physics under coordinate transformations including boosts.
Second postulate added; 'special' because gravity and non-inertial frames are excluded.
Covariance glossed as equations keeping their form with no new terms after transformation.
Speed limit c turns into forward and backward light cones; identical orientation of all cones is the mark of flat spacetime.

sections.title: What is general relativity?
sections.summary: Recounts Newton's inverse-square gravity and its success, then the philosophical gap: no mechanism for how influence crosses empty space, which Newton himself admitted. Einstein's resolution is that gravity is the curvature of spacetime determined by matter, summarized by Wheeler's two-line slogan. A field is defined as a map from spacetime points to amplitudes (scalar, vector, tensor); GR is a classical field theory whose uniqueness is that matter-field energy couples to the metric field, the geometry itself. Einstein's equation is stated in words (curvature = matter energy density), and the section closes on Einstein's struggle with unfamiliar geometry, Grossmann's help and Cartan's later reformulation, motivating the book's early mathematical chapters.
key_moves: Contrast 'how gravity behaves' (Newton) with 'what gravity is' (missing mechanism).
Replace a transmitted force by geometry that matter shapes and that guides motion.
Field as a machine from position to amplitude; the metric is the special field.
Einstein equation split into a geometric left side and a physical right side.
Historical note that the mathematical barrier, not the physics, is the source of the theory's reputation.

sections.title: What is a metric?
sections.summary: The metric field is described as the local rulebook for distances and angles between events in the unified entity spacetime, expressed through a line element for nearby events. Euclid's unprovable parallel postulate and the later discovery of consistent non-Euclidean geometries give an operational test for curvature: initially parallel lines converge or diverge. Physically, relative motion of two nearby neutral test particles launched in parallel signals gravity. The metric varies from point to point, the Einstein equation is a differential equation for it, and curvature comes from how the metric changes.
key_moves: Metric as distance-and-angle rules, local to each event.
Line element as the practical way to write a metric, enabling thought experiments with assumed geometries.
Parallel postulate failure equals curvature; convergence or divergence measures it.
Translate geometric non-parallelism into relative motion of free test particles.
Metric as a field: insert an event, get back the local distance rule; Einstein's equation governs its variation.

sections.title: What are we building on?
sections.summary: Because GR must reproduce Newton for weak fields and slow motion, the section rebuilds Newtonian gravity in field language: force law, field g = F/m, conservative field and potential Phi = -GM/r. Example 0.3 weighs the Earth using g, R and Cavendish's G and gets its density; the same logic with the Earth's orbit gives the Sun's mass and density, and Fig. 6 shows how the Earth-Sun distance was first estimated from the half-Moon angle. The Sun estimate and the following escape-speed argument are still set inside the Example 0.3 box, in small type across the page break. Equating kinetic energy to potential depth gives escape speed and the radius R = c/sqrt(8 pi G rho) at which light could not escape, deemed implausible for ordinary densities. Flux through a sphere plus the divergence theorem and a Dirac delta give div g = -4 pi G M delta, generalized by linearity to div g = -4 pi G rho and Poisson's equation. Phi/c^2 near unity signals Newton's breakdown, but Example 0.4 notes GPS time dilation and Mercury's 43 arcsec per century perihelion excess as measurable relativistic effects in weak fields.
key_moves: Force per unit mass defines a vector field; conservative, so it is minus the gradient of a scalar potential.
Invert g = GM/R^2 to weigh the Earth once G is measured; divide by volume for density.
Circular-orbit balance v^2 = GM/R with v = 2 pi R/tau gives the Sun's mass from one year and one AU.
Escape speed grows linearly with radius at fixed density; setting it to c yields a radius larger than an AU for solar-system densities.
Flux of g through a sphere is -4 pi G M independent of radius; the divergence theorem converts it to a local law with a delta-function source.
Linearity turns the point-mass result into an integral over density and Poisson's equation.
Dimensions of Phi are velocity squared, so Phi/c^2 is the natural dimensionless measure of relativistic gravity.
Counterpoint: GR effects are measurable even when Phi/c^2 is tiny (GPS clocks, Mercury's orbit).

sections.title: Who is this book for?
sections.summary: Describes the intended reader (curious, undergraduate physics background, not aiming to be a professional relativist), acknowledges two reader types (physics-first and mathematics-first), recommends that beginners work through at least Chapters 1-13, and lays out the six Parts: flat-spacetime geometry and the metric; curvature and the field equation; cosmology; stars, black holes and orbits; formal geometry; field theory and quantum links. A margin box explains that curved-arrow boxes flag optional detours.
key_moves: Offer two reading paths and a minimum core.
Announce the spiral: formal geometry in Part V revisits tools met informally in Parts I-II.

sections.title: Units in this book
sections.summary: SI units are used at first, then geometrized units with G = c = 1 are phased in (c = 1 from Chapter 2, G = 1 from Part III), with frequent translation back to 'real-world' units. Example 0.5 shows that c converts time to length and G/c^2 converts mass to length; the general rule maps L^n T^m M^p to L^(n+m+p) with factor c^m (G/c^2)^p, tabulated for common quantities. Example 0.6 restores constants in G = 8 pi T to get G = (8 pi G/c^4) T.
key_moves: Identify c (L/T) and G/c^2 (L/M) as the two conversion keys.
Generalize to a one-line exponent rule and a table.
Check both sides of the field equation have dimension L^-2 in geometrized units, then insert G/c^4 on the matter side.

sections.title: Exercises
sections.summary: Three Newtonian estimation problems: the escape-speed route to the Schwarzschild radius, surface gravity and escape speed for Earth, Sun and a neutron star, and head-to-foot tidal forces on a person on Earth and at the horizon radius of stellar-mass and supermassive black holes.
key_moves: Push Newtonian formulas into regimes where Phi/c^2 is no longer small, to motivate GR.

concepts.name: general relativity
concepts.definition: Einstein's classical field theory of gravitation in which gravity is the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime, the curvature being determined by the energy and momentum of matter and fields.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced through its scope (cosmology, black holes, gravitational waves) and contrasted with Newtonian gravity's lack of mechanism.

concepts.name: inertial reference frame
concepts.definition: A non-accelerating frame of reference, i.e. one in which a body subject to no force moves in a straight line at constant speed.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined via Newton's first law; illustrated by juggling on a fixed floor or a smoothly moving train.

concepts.name: principle of relativity
concepts.definition: The laws of physics take the same form in every inertial reference frame, so no experiment can single out a state of absolute rest.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a box as a consequence of Newton's first law holding in all inertial frames, then reinterpreted as a symmetry principle.
concepts.notes: Pre-Einsteinian; accepted by Galileo and Newton.

concepts.name: rest frame
concepts.definition: The frame of reference in which a given particle is at rest.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note used to sharpen the claim that Newtonian physics has no absolute rest frame.

concepts.name: boost
concepts.definition: A change of coordinates to a frame moving with constant velocity relative to the original one.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed alongside rotations and translations as a transformation under which physics is unchanged; Example 0.2 (the neighbouring-train illusion) makes it tangible.

concepts.name: principle of invariant light speed
concepts.definition: In every inertial frame light travels through vacuum at the same speed c, regardless of how the source moves.
concepts.how_introduced: Added as Einstein's 1905 postulate on top of the principle of relativity, with consequences deferred to Chapter 1.

concepts.name: special relativity
concepts.definition: The theory built on the principle of relativity and the invariance of light speed, restricted to inertial frames and neglecting gravity; its spacetime is flat.
concepts.how_introduced: Named 'special' because it covers only the special case of inertial frames without gravity.

concepts.name: covariance
concepts.definition: A theory is covariant under a group of coordinate changes when its equations look identical in the new coordinates: rewriting them generates no extra terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Glossed in the text as transforming "sensibly"; a margin note then makes that precise as unchanged equation form.
concepts.notes: Distinct from invariance of individual quantities; the chapter does not draw this distinction.

concepts.name: Lorentz transformation
concepts.definition: The linear coordinate transformation between inertial frames that keeps the speed of light the same in both; replaces the Galilean boost.
concepts.how_introduced: Named only, as the correct way to perform boosts consistent with the light postulate; derived in Chapter 1.

concepts.name: Lorentz covariance
concepts.definition: The property that the equations of a theory keep their form under Lorentz transformations (together with translations, rotations and reflections).
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the symmetry content of special relativity.

concepts.name: spacetime diagram
concepts.definition: A plot with time on the vertical axis and one or two spatial coordinates horizontal, in which events are points and histories are world lines.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to draw the speed-of-light limit as a cone (Fig. 2).

concepts.name: light cone
concepts.definition: The set of events reachable by light signals to or from a given event; its interior and surface bound all events that event can influence (future cone) or be influenced by (past cone).
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as a double cone on a spacetime diagram; illustrated with a thrown stone or torch beam (future) and starlight or an assassin's bullet (past).

concepts.name: flat spacetime
concepts.definition: Spacetime without curvature, the arena of special relativity, in which coordinates can be chosen so that every event's light cone has the same orientation and opening angle.
concepts.how_introduced: Pictured as a regular lattice of identical upright cones, like soldiers on parade (Fig. 3a).

concepts.name: curved spacetime
concepts.definition: Spacetime whose geometry cannot be made globally flat by any choice of coordinates; nearby free particles accelerate relative to one another and light cones cannot all be aligned.
concepts.how_introduced: Pictured as light cones tipped at irregular angles, like soldiers who have been drinking (Fig. 3b); linked to gravity in §0.2.

concepts.name: equivalence principle
concepts.definition: Locally, the effects of a uniform gravitational field cannot be distinguished from those of uniform acceleration of the reference frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Foreshadowed in Example 0.1: a juggler in a steadily accelerating train can compensate as if gravity were a bit stronger.

concepts.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
concepts.definition: Two point masses M and m separated by r attract along the line joining them with force of magnitude GMm/r^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Given first as the historic unification of falling apples and the orbiting Moon (§0.2), then in vector form eqn 2 (§0.4).

concepts.name: gravitational constant G
concepts.definition: The constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, about 6.674 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2.
concepts.how_introduced: Value given in a margin note with attribution to Cavendish's 1798 torsion-balance measurement.

concepts.name: action at a distance
concepts.definition: The Newtonian picture in which a mass influences another across empty space with no intervening mechanism or propagation.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the flaw in Newton's theory that troubled seventeenth-century mechanists and Newton himself (margin note quoting his 1717 Opticks preface).

concepts.name: spacetime curvature as gravity
concepts.definition: Gravity is not a force propagating through spacetime but the curvature of spacetime itself: matter-energy determines the curvature, and curvature determines how free bodies move.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as Einstein's answer to Newton's missing mechanism, compressed into Wheeler's two-line summary and pointed at Fig. 3(b).

concepts.name: field
concepts.definition: A rule assigning to every point of spacetime a quantity (scalar, vector or tensor) giving the amplitude of something at that point.
concepts.how_introduced: Described as a machine that eats a spacetime position and outputs an amplitude; examples are the electromagnetic, particle and fluid fields.

concepts.name: classical field theory
concepts.definition: A field theory in which fields are ordinary (non-quantized) functions on spacetime; general relativity is one.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note, which glosses 'classical' as not compatible with quantum mechanics and points ahead to Chapter 49.
concepts.notes: The book's gloss conflates 'not quantized' with 'incompatible with quantum mechanics'; see gaps.

concepts.name: matter fields
concepts.definition: All non-gravitational fields, including those of massive particles and fluids and massless fields such as electromagnetism, whose energy acts as the source of gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note defining the term used on the right-hand side of the word equation.

concepts.name: metric field
concepts.definition: A field on spacetime that at each event supplies the rule for computing intervals (distances, times) and angles between neighbouring events; its variation from place to place encodes curvature and hence gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Singled out in §0.2 as the special field to which matter energy couples, then explained in §0.3 as a local rulebook that returns a distance formula when fed a position.
concepts.notes: Made precise as g_{mu nu} in GA ch5.

concepts.name: Einstein field equation
concepts.definition: The equation relating spacetime curvature (built from the metric and its derivatives) to the energy-momentum content of matter fields; in geometrized units G = 8 pi T.
concepts.how_introduced: Written first as a word equation, curvature on the left equal to matter energy density on the right, then in §0.6 with tensor symbols for unit conversion.

concepts.name: spacetime
concepts.definition: The single four-dimensional continuum formed by space and time together, whose points are events.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a consequence of the metric linking space and time inseparably; margin note warns that coordinates, including t, lose intrinsic meaning.

concepts.name: event
concepts.definition: A point of spacetime: a particular place at a particular instant.
concepts.how_introduced: Named as the spacetime analogue of a point between which the metric gives distances.

concepts.name: line element
concepts.definition: An expression for the squared interval between two infinitesimally separated events in terms of coordinate differentials and the metric components.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the practical way of writing down a metric, allowing one to posit a geometry and explore its consequences.
concepts.notes: No explicit formula is given in this chapter.

concepts.name: parallel postulate
concepts.definition: Euclid's assumption that lines which start parallel remain parallel indefinitely; it holds in flat geometry but fails in curved spaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Historical route: Euclid could not prove it, and later geometers found consistent geometries without it.

concepts.name: curvature
concepts.definition: The departure of a geometry from flatness, detected by the convergence or divergence of initially parallel straight lines (geodesics) and quantified by how the metric varies.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined operationally from failure of the parallel postulate, then linked to the Einstein equation as a differential equation for the metric.
concepts.notes: Made precise with the Riemann tensor in GA ch11.

concepts.name: geodesic deviation
concepts.definition: The relative acceleration of neighbouring freely falling test particles whose paths start parallel; it vanishes in flat spacetime and measures curvature (tidal gravity).
concepts.how_introduced: Physical restatement of the parallel-lines test: two small uncharged test particles started parallel at the same speed drift relative to each other only if gravity is present.
concepts.notes: Strictly, a uniform field produces no relative motion; only tidal (non-uniform) gravity does.

concepts.name: coordinate independence
concepts.definition: Coordinates are arbitrary labels of events with no intrinsic physical meaning; physical content lies in geometric quantities such as intervals.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note stating that treating spacetime as one entity demotes coordinates, including the time label t.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit
concepts.definition: General relativity must reproduce Newtonian gravity when fields are weak and speeds are much smaller than c.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the justification for reviewing Newtonian gravity in §0.4 (margin note 15).

concepts.name: gravitational field
concepts.definition: The vector field g(r) giving gravitational force per unit test mass at each position; for a point mass it points radially inward with magnitude GM/r^2.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by dividing the force law by m, drawn as inward arrows on a circle (Fig. 4).

concepts.name: conservative force field
concepts.definition: A force field for which the work done around any closed path is zero, so it can be written as minus the gradient of a scalar potential.
concepts.how_introduced: Illustrated by the work to roll a ball uphill equalling the energy released when it rolls back down.

concepts.name: gravitational potential
concepts.definition: The scalar field Phi(r) with g = -grad Phi; for a point mass Phi = -GM/r, and it has dimensions of velocity squared.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced from the conservative nature of g with the conventional minus sign; plotted as a -1/r well (Fig. 5).

concepts.name: shell theorem
concepts.definition: Outside a spherically symmetric mass distribution, the field and potential are identical to those of a point mass with the same total mass at the centre.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a consequence of Gauss's theorem, to justify treating Earth and Sun as point masses.

concepts.name: Cavendish experiment
concepts.definition: Cavendish's 1798 torsion-balance measurement of the tiny attraction between lead spheres, which fixes G and so allows the Earth's mass to be deduced from surface gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 0.3 turns it into a calculation of Earth's mass and density.

concepts.name: astronomical unit
concepts.definition: The mean Earth-Sun distance, about 1.496 x 10^11 m.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in the Sun-mass estimate inside the Example 0.3 box, with the half-Moon angle method (Fig. 6) and transit-of-Venus parallax as historical routes.

concepts.name: escape velocity
concepts.definition: The minimum launch speed from the surface of a body for a projectile to reach infinity, found by equating kinetic energy to the depth of the potential well: sqrt(2GM/R).
concepts.how_introduced: Worked out in a couple of lines at the end of the long Example 0.3 box (the dark-star remark), then revisited in Exercises 0.1-0.2.

concepts.name: Newtonian dark star
concepts.definition: A hypothetical body so compact that its Newtonian escape speed exceeds c, so light cannot leave it; for uniform density this needs R >= c/sqrt(8 pi G rho), equivalently R <= 2GM/c^2 at fixed mass.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why, with solar-system densities, black holes looked implausible in the nineteenth century: the required radius exceeds an AU.
concepts.notes: The book does not name Michell or Laplace here; GA ch25 credits both in its opening margin note.

concepts.name: divergence theorem
concepts.definition: The flux of a vector field out of a closed surface equals the volume integral of the field's divergence over the enclosed region.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from vector calculus to turn the sphere-flux result into a local differential law.

concepts.name: Dirac delta function
concepts.definition: A distribution concentrated at the origin with unit integral, defined by integrating against a test function to give the function's value at the origin; the three-dimensional version is the product of three one-dimensional deltas.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note used to represent a point mass as a density so that Gauss's law can be written locally.

concepts.name: Gauss's law for gravity
concepts.definition: The flux of the gravitational field through any closed surface equals -4 pi G times the enclosed mass; locally, div g = -4 pi G rho.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed first for a sphere around a point mass (radius drops out), then converted and generalized in margin note 19.

concepts.name: superposition in Newtonian gravity
concepts.definition: Because Newton's equations are linear in mass, the field or potential of any distribution is the sum (integral) of point-mass contributions.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked to pass from a point mass to an arbitrary density via eqn 13.
concepts.notes: Contrast with GR, whose field equation is nonlinear (not stated here).

concepts.name: Poisson's equation for gravity
concepts.definition: The Laplacian of the gravitational potential equals 4 pi G times the mass density; it is the Newtonian analogue of Einstein's field equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by substituting g = -grad Phi into div g = -4 pi G rho, and compared with Poisson's equation in electrostatics.
concepts.notes: Used again in GA ch6 and ch13 as the target the Einstein equation must reduce to.

concepts.name: relativistic strength parameter Phi/c^2
aliases: gravitational potential in units of c^2
concepts.definition: The dimensionless ratio |Phi|/c^2 comparing gravitational potential energy per unit mass to rest energy per unit mass; when it approaches order unity Newtonian gravity fails badly.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by noting Phi has dimensions of velocity squared, then tempered by examples where GR effects matter even when the ratio is tiny.

concepts.name: gravitational time dilation
concepts.definition: Clocks deeper in a gravitational potential run slow relative to clocks higher up.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in Example 0.4 as measurable at the Earth's surface and needed for GPS accuracy.

concepts.name: perihelion precession of Mercury
concepts.definition: The slow rotation of Mercury's orbital ellipse, about 575 arcsec per century, of which about 532 is explained by Newtonian perturbations from other planets; the remaining 43 arcsec per century is accounted for by general relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 0.4 uses it to show relativistic effects can matter at speeds well under a thousandth of c, and ties it ironically to the Carlyle epigraph.
concepts.notes: Calculated in GA ch23; listed among triumphs in GA ch14.

concepts.name: neutron star
concepts.definition: A collapsed stellar remnant with nuclear-scale density, supported largely by neutron degeneracy pressure, typically about 1.4 solar masses in a radius of order 10 km.
concepts.how_introduced: Margin note 17 says such dense compact objects could only be understood after quantum mechanics, undercutting the nineteenth-century density argument; used in Exercise 0.2.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild radius
concepts.definition: The radius 2GM/c^2 associated with mass M; in GR it marks a non-rotating black hole's event horizon, and by coincidence it equals the Newtonian radius at which escape speed reaches c.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached in Exercise 0.1 by setting the Newtonian escape speed equal to c.

concepts.name: tidal force
concepts.definition: The difference in gravitational force across an extended body due to the field's variation with position, roughly 2GMm h/r^3 along the radial direction for a body of length h.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 0.3 (head-to-feet difference on a human), pointing ahead to curvature.

concepts.name: geometrized units
concepts.definition: A unit system in which G and c are set to 1, so time, mass and energy are all measured in lengths; equations lose explicit G and c factors.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by simplification of equations, balanced against numerical confusion; phased in gradually with frequent return to SI ('real-world') units.

concepts.name: dimensional conversion factor
aliases: unit conversion rule for geometrized units
concepts.definition: A real-world quantity with dimensions L^n T^m M^p becomes a length power L^(n+m+p) in geometrized units after multiplication by c^m (G/c^2)^p.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from the two keys c (L/T) and G/c^2 (L/M) in Example 0.5, then tabulated and applied to the field equation.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: The curvature tensor on the geometric side of the field equation, built from the Ricci tensor and scalar; it has dimensions of inverse length squared.
concepts.how_introduced: Named only in Example 0.6, with a caution not to confuse the bold tensor G with the constant G.

concepts.name: energy-momentum tensor
concepts.definition: The tensor describing the density and flux of energy and momentum of matter fields; it sources curvature in Einstein's equation.
concepts.how_introduced: Named only in Example 0.6 as the tensor with dimensions of energy density on the matter side; caution not to confuse bold T with temperature.

key_equations.name: Light cone surface
key_equations.meaning: Events reachable by light signals from the origin; boundary between causally connected and disconnected events.
key_equations.symbols: x,y,z spatial coordinates; t time; c speed of light

key_equations.name: Newton's gravitation (magnitude)
key_equations.meaning: Magnitude of the attraction between two point masses.
key_equations.symbols: G gravitational constant; M,m masses; r separation

key_equations.name: Einstein equation in words
key_equations.meaning: Geometry on the left is determined by matter-energy on the right; the conceptual form of GR.

key_equations.name: Newton's law in vector form
key_equations.meaning: Force on m at r from M at the origin; minus sign expresses attraction.

key_equations.name: Definition of gravitational field
key_equations.meaning: Gravitational field is force per unit mass, independent of the test mass.

key_equations.name: Point-mass field
key_equations.meaning: Inward-pointing inverse-square vector field around a point mass (Fig. 4).

key_equations.name: Field from potential
key_equations.meaning: Conservative field written as minus the gradient of a scalar potential.

key_equations.name: Point-mass potential
key_equations.meaning: Potential well of a point mass (Fig. 5); also valid outside any spherical mass.

key_equations.name: Weighing the Earth
key_equations.meaning: Earth's mass from surface gravity, radius and G.

key_equations.name: Mean density
key_equations.meaning: Mean density of a sphere; gives 5.5e3 kg m^-3 for Earth and 1.4e3 kg m^-3 for the Sun.

key_equations.name: Circular orbit balance
key_equations.meaning: Gravity supplies the centripetal force for Earth's nearly circular orbit.
key_equations.symbols: R_ES astronomical unit; v orbital speed; tau period

key_equations.name: Solar mass from Kepler's third law (rearranged, not printed)
key_equations.meaning: Combining the two orbit relations; with tau = 1 yr gives 1.99e30 kg.

key_equations.name: Escape speed
key_equations.meaning: Launch speed needed to climb out of the potential well; at fixed density it grows linearly with radius.

key_equations.name: Dark-star radius
key_equations.meaning: Radius at which Newtonian escape speed equals c for a body of density rho.

key_equations.name: Flux through a sphere
key_equations.meaning: Inverse-square fall-off cancels the area growth, so the flux is independent of radius.

key_equations.name: Divergence theorem applied to g
key_equations.meaning: Surface flux equals volume integral of divergence.

key_equations.name: Delta-function normalization
key_equations.meaning: Unit total weight of the delta function.

key_equations.name: Delta-function sifting property
key_equations.latex: \int d^d x\, f(\vec x)\,\delta^{(d)}(\vec x) = f(0)
key_equations.meaning: Defining property of the delta function.

key_equations.name: Local Gauss law for a point mass
key_equations.meaning: Divergence of g vanishes except at the point mass, where it is a delta spike of strength -4 pi G M.

key_equations.name: Potential of a mass distribution
key_equations.latex: \Phi(\vec r) = -\int \frac{G\rho(\vec r')}{|\vec r-\vec r'|}\, d^3 r'
key_equations.meaning: Superposition of point-mass potentials.

key_equations.name: Density as superposed point masses (margin note 19)
key_equations.latex: \rho(\vec r) \equiv \int \rho(\vec r')\,\delta(\vec r-\vec r')\, d^3 r'
key_equations.meaning: Any density can be viewed as a continuum of delta-function point masses.

key_equations.name: Gauss's theorem for gravity, integral form (margin note 19)
key_equations.latex: \int_S \vec g\cdot d\vec S = -4\pi G M,\qquad M = \int\rho(\vec r')\,d^3 r'
key_equations.meaning: Flux through any closed surface depends only on enclosed mass.

key_equations.name: Local Gauss law for gravity
key_equations.meaning: Mass density is the local source of gravitational field lines.

key_equations.name: Poisson's equation for gravity
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian field equation: second derivatives of the potential set by mass density. GR must reduce to it.

key_equations.name: Electrostatic analogues (margin note 20)
key_equations.latex:
\vec F = q\vec E,\quad \vec E = -\vec
abla\phi,\quad \oint_S\vec E\cdot d\vec S = Q/\epsilon_0,\quad \vec
abla\cdot\vec E = ho/\epsilon_0,\quad 
abla^2\phi = -ho/\epsilon_0
key_equations.meaning: Same mathematical structure as Newtonian gravity with opposite sign (like charges repel).
key_equations.symbols: The printed note writes the potential as V in Poisson's equation but phi elsewhere.

key_equations.name: Newtonian breakdown criterion
key_equations.meaning: When gravitational potential energy rivals rest energy, relativistic gravity becomes essential.

key_equations.name: Geometrized conversion rule
key_equations.meaning: One rule for converting any quantity between SI and G = c = 1 units.
key_equations.symbols: L length, T time, M mass dimensions

key_equations.name: Einstein equation, geometrized units
key_equations.meaning: Einstein tensor equals 8 pi times energy-momentum tensor when G = c = 1.
key_equations.symbols: bold G Einstein tensor; bold T energy-momentum tensor

key_equations.name: Einstein equation, SI units
key_equations.meaning: Restoring constants: curvature (L^-2) equals G/c^4 times energy density.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild radius (Exercise 0.1 target)
key_equations.meaning: Radius at which Newtonian escape speed equals c; coincides with the GR horizon radius.

figures.label: Fig. 1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Juggling works fine in an inertial frame or one with steady acceleration.
figures.visual_description: Cartoon line drawing of a clown with a big hat, spotted trousers, braces and oversized shoes standing on a flat plank, arms spread, juggling four balls that trace a neat arc above his head with small motion streaks.
figures.what_it_teaches: In a frame with no jolting, projectiles follow predictable Newtonian parabolas, so physics is simple.

redesign.idea: Frame-switching juggling lab: a juggler on a platform whose motion can be set to rest, constant velocity, constant acceleration or random jolts, with ball trajectories drawn both in the platform frame and the ground frame.
redesign.interaction: Learner picks the platform motion mode and acceleration value and toggles the viewing frame; ball paths, a 'predicted parabola' overlay and a catch/miss counter update live. Constant acceleration shows parabolas with a tilted effective g.

figures.label: Fig. 1(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Juggling fails when the frame's acceleration changes with time.
figures.visual_description: The same clown cartoon tumbling sideways in mid-air, hat flying off, balls scattered in different directions, above a plank flanked by double-headed motion marks; a horizontal arrow below labelled a(t) shows the platform's time-varying acceleration.
figures.what_it_teaches: Time-varying acceleration introduces extra, unpredictable fictitious forces, so a non-uniformly accelerating frame cannot be treated like an inertial one plus a constant gravitational field.

redesign.idea: Same juggling lab in jolt mode, plotting a(t) under the scene so learners see catches fail exactly when the acceleration changes.
redesign.interaction: Learner draws an a(t) curve with the mouse; the simulation replays and marks the fictitious force on each ball as an arrow.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A light cone on a spacetime diagram with time vertical and two space directions horizontal; the observer at the apex can affect events in the future cone and be affected by events in the past cone.
figures.visual_description: A stippled double cone meeting at its apex, drawn in perspective with elliptical rims top and bottom. A vertical arrow on the left is labelled 'time'; a small pair of axes on the right labelled x and y indicates the horizontal spatial plane. The top rim carries the label sqrt(x^2+y^2+z^2) = c|t|. The inventory attaches the Fig. 3 caption to this image; it is actually Fig. 2.
figures.what_it_teaches: The finite speed of light partitions spacetime around an event into causal future, causal past and elsewhere.

redesign.idea: 3D light-cone explorer: an observer at the origin, with draggable events that colour themselves future, past or elsewhere; a flash of light expands as a circle whose history sweeps out the cone.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags events and the camera, and scrubs a time slider; a panel reports whether a signal slower than or equal to c can connect the event to the origin.

figures.label: Fig. 3(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: In flat spacetime light cones at different points all line up like soldiers on parade.
figures.visual_description: A 3-by-4 grid of identical small hourglass-shaped double cones, all upright with vertical axes and equal opening angles, drawn in light grey pencil with dashed rear rims.
figures.what_it_teaches: Uniform, identically oriented cones everywhere is the picture of flat spacetime, where one global inertial description works.

redesign.idea: Light-cone field viewer paired with Fig. 3(b): a grid of cones computed from a chosen metric, starting from Minkowski where every cone is identical.
redesign.interaction: Learner selects a metric (Minkowski, Schwarzschild in Schwarzschild coordinates, Eddington-Finkelstein, Rindler) and a mass slider; cones re-tilt and narrow, with a toggle to switch to local inertial coordinates at any clicked point, which restores an upright cone there.

figures.label: Fig. 3(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: In curved spacetime the light cones look disorderly, like soldiers who have been drinking.
figures.visual_description: The same 3-by-4 arrangement of double cones, but the left columns are strongly tipped over toward the left (almost lying on their sides), the second column tipped less, and the right-hand columns nearly upright, giving an impression of cones progressively leaning more toward one side of the grid.
figures.what_it_teaches: Gravity (curvature) shows up as a position-dependent orientation of the causal structure that cannot be undone everywhere at once.

redesign.idea: Same viewer as Fig. 3(a) in curved mode, with a probe that tries to align all cones by a coordinate change and reports that it can only do so near one point.
redesign.interaction: Learner clicks a point to straighten its cone; neighbouring cones stay straight only to first order and the residual misalignment grows with distance, displayed as a heat map proportional to curvature.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Gravitational field vectors around a point mass M.
figures.visual_description: A dotted circle with a dot labelled M at its centre. Twelve short black arrows sit on the circle at equal angular spacing, each pointing radially inward toward M. A label g(r) with vector arrows sits near the upper right arrow.
figures.what_it_teaches: The Newtonian field is a radial, inward vector field of equal magnitude on each sphere around the mass.

redesign.idea: Flux-and-field sandbox: place point masses on a 2D/3D canvas, see the g vector field as arrows whose length follows 1/r^2, and draw closed surfaces whose total flux is computed live.
redesign.interaction: Learner drags masses and resizes or reshapes a Gaussian surface; the flux readout stays at -4 pi G times the enclosed mass and jumps only when a mass crosses the surface.

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Gravitational potential of a point mass plotted against distance.
figures.visual_description: Axes with Phi(r) vertical and r horizontal; the r-axis sits at the top (Phi = 0). A thick curve plunges toward minus infinity near r = 0 and rises monotonically toward the axis from below as r grows, approaching zero asymptotically. The label -GM/r sits under the curve.
figures.what_it_teaches: The potential is a negative, bottomless 1/r well; escape requires filling the well's depth with kinetic energy.

redesign.idea: Potential-well launcher: plot -GM/r with a planet surface marker at R, and a ball launched with adjustable speed whose total energy is drawn as a horizontal line.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets M, R and launch speed; the energy line either stays below zero (bound, ball returns) or reaches zero (escape), with a secondary axis showing |Phi|/c^2 and a flag when the escape speed would exceed c.

figures.label: Fig. 6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Not-to-scale sketch of estimating the Sun's distance from the angle between the Sun and a half-Moon, in astronomical units.
figures.visual_description: A right triangle with circles at its corners: the Moon at upper left (half dark, half lit, lit side toward the Sun), a radiant Sun labelled S at right, and the Earth labelled E at lower left. The Moon-Sun side is labelled 1, the short Earth-Moon side 0.00257, and the angle at Earth between the Moon and Sun directions 89.853 degrees. The right angle is at the Moon.
figures.what_it_teaches: At half-Moon the Earth-Moon-Sun angle at the Moon is 90 degrees, so measuring the Moon-Sun angle from Earth and knowing the lunar distance gives the Sun's distance by trigonometry; the angle is extremely close to 90 degrees.

redesign.idea: Aristarchus triangle: a draggable Moon phase and an angle gauge showing how the inferred Sun distance depends sensitively on the measured angle.
redesign.interaction: Learner adjusts the measured angle (e.g. from 87 to 89.853 degrees); the implied Earth-Sun to Earth-Moon ratio (1/cos angle) updates from about 19 to about 390, illustrating why ancient estimates were far too small.

figures.label: Units conversion table (§0.6)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Dimensions of common quantities in SI and in geometrized units, with the factor that converts between them.
figures.visual_description: A typeset table with horizontal rules and four columns: the quantity name, its SI dimension written in sans-serif L, T, M powers, its dimension once G = c = 1, and the multiplying factor. Eight rows cover length, time, mass, velocity, energy, energy density, mass density and pressure. Reading down the geometrized column, everything collapses to a length power: time, mass and energy become lengths, velocity becomes dimensionless, and the three densities/pressure become inverse area. The factor column shows only 1, c, 1/c, G/c^2 and G/c^4. Exported as an HTML table, not an image.
figures.what_it_teaches: Every quantity collapses to a power of length when G = c = 1, with a systematic multiplicative factor.

redesign.idea: Geometrized-units converter: enter any SI quantity (or pick the Sun, a neutron star, 1 second, 1 joule) and see its length-equivalent with the factor built up exponent by exponent.
redesign.interaction: Learner sets n, m, p exponents or chooses a preset; the tool shows c^m (G/c^2)^p symbolically and numerically, and a reverse mode restores c and G into a pasted geometrized formula such as G = 8 pi T or r = 2M.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.1
worked_examples.problem: Explain in which kinds of moving frame a juggler can still use simple Newtonian reasoning to catch balls.
worked_examples.method: Qualitative case analysis over four frames: stationary floor, train at constant velocity, train at constant acceleration, jolting train.
worked_examples.key_insight: Uniform velocity changes nothing (principle of relativity, basis of SR); uniform acceleration is equivalent to an extra uniform gravitational field and can be compensated (seed of the equivalence principle); only time-varying acceleration spoils simple laws.
worked_examples.result: Juggling works in inertial and uniformly accelerating frames, fails under jolts.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.2
worked_examples.problem: Illustrate everyday insensitivity of physics to boosts.
worked_examples.method: Describe sitting in a stationary train while a neighbouring train pulls away, and the need to look at the platform to decide which train moved.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only relative motion is perceptible without an external reference, so the station frame and the boosted frame are physically on an equal footing.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.3
worked_examples.problem: Determine the Earth's mass and mean density from surface gravity, Earth's radius and the Cavendish value of G.
worked_examples.method: Set mg = GM m/R^2 from eqn 4 to get M = gR^2/G, then divide by the sphere volume.
worked_examples.key_insight: Measuring G in the lab is what converts known accelerations into masses: 'weighing the world'.
worked_examples.result: M_earth = 5.97e24 kg; mean density 5.5e3 kg m^-3, about 5.5 times water.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.3 (continued)
worked_examples.problem: Estimate the Sun's mass and mean density from the length of the year and the astronomical unit.
worked_examples.method: Treat Earth's orbit as circular, equate gravitational and centripetal forces to get v^2 = GM/R, combine with tau = 2 pi R/v and tau = 1 yr, then divide by the Sun's volume using R_sun = 6.96e8 m. (Printed in small type inside the Example 0.3 box, which runs over from p. 6 to p. 7.)
worked_examples.key_insight: A planet's orbit weighs its star; the Earth's own mass cancels.
worked_examples.result: M_sun = 1.99e30 kg; density about 1.4e3 kg m^-3; M_sun/M_earth = 3.33e5 and R_sun/R_earth = 1.09e2 (margin data box).

worked_examples.label: Example 0.3 (continued, dark star)
worked_examples.problem: How large must a body of given mean density be for its Newtonian escape speed to reach c?
worked_examples.method: Equate kinetic energy at launch to potential well depth GMm/R, write M = (4/3) pi rho R^3, and solve v_esc = c for R. (Still inside the Example 0.3 box; the box closes after the remark that eqn 7 seemed unattainable, and margin note 17 hangs off that remark.)
worked_examples.key_insight: At fixed density escape speed grows in proportion to radius, so trapping light needs either enormous size or enormous density; solar-system densities would require radii beyond an AU.
worked_examples.result: R = c/sqrt(8 pi G rho). Own check: rho = 1000 kg m^-3 gives about 2.3e11 m (1.5 AU); rho = 5500 kg m^-3 gives about 1e11 m (0.66 AU).

worked_examples.problem: Derive the local (differential) form of Newton's law of gravity from the point-mass field.
worked_examples.method: Integrate g over a sphere of radius R (flux = -4 pi G M, independent of R); apply the divergence theorem; represent the point mass with a 3D Dirac delta to get div g = -4 pi G M delta(r); superpose via density to obtain div g = -4 pi G rho and substitute g = -grad Phi.
worked_examples.key_insight: Inverse-square fall-off is exactly what makes flux depend only on enclosed mass, allowing a local field equation with mass density as source.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.4
worked_examples.problem: Give cases where relativistic gravity matters although |Phi| is far below c^2.
worked_examples.method: Two short case studies: gravitational time dilation for GPS; the budget of Mercury's perihelion precession (575 total, 532 Newtonian perturbations, 43 unexplained arcsec per century).
worked_examples.key_insight: Small relativistic corrections become important when measurements are very precise (clocks) or when effects accumulate over many orbits (precession).
worked_examples.result: Residual 43 arcsec per century explained by GR; Mercury's speed 47 km/s is below 0.0002c.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.5
worked_examples.problem: Find the factors that turn SI times and masses into lengths in geometrized units.
worked_examples.method: Inside the box: c has dimensions L/T and G/c^2 has L/M, so multiply a time by c and a mass by G/c^2 to get lengths. Directly after the box, the main text generalizes: L^n T^m M^p becomes L^(n+m+p) with factor c^m (G/c^2)^p, and gives a table of eight quantities.
worked_examples.key_insight: Setting G = c = 1 is not new physics, only choosing units where c and G/c^2 are dimensionless conversion rates.
worked_examples.result: Inside the box: time multiplied by c, mass by G/c^2. In the following table: velocity c^-1, energy, energy density and pressure G/c^4, mass density G/c^2.

worked_examples.label: Example 0.6
worked_examples.problem: Restore G and c in the geometrized field equation G = 8 pi T.
worked_examples.method: Identify dimensions: the curvature side is L^-2 (factor 1), the matter side is an energy density (factor G/c^4); multiply each side by its factor.
worked_examples.key_insight: The coupling constant 8 pi G/c^4 is tiny, which is why enormous energy densities are needed for appreciable curvature.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A juggler on a floor, a smooth train, an accelerating train and a jolting train
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Each setting tests whether ball trajectories remain predictable, sorting frames into inertial, uniformly accelerated (gravity-like) and hopeless.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Uniform acceleration is only locally equivalent to gravity; real gravitational fields vary in space (tides), which the juggler cannot remove.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: The frame-switching juggling lab described under Fig. 1, with a tidal mode showing balls drifting apart in a non-uniform field.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The neighbouring-train illusion in a station
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows that without an external reference one cannot tell which of two uniformly moving frames is 'really' moving.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The illusion occurs during the gentle start-up (a small acceleration) and relies on limited peripheral cues; strictly it illustrates relative velocity perception.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-window view from two trains with a hidden platform; the learner guesses which train moves, then reveals the platform.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Light cones as soldiers on parade, orderly when sober and staggering when drunk
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Aligned cones depict flat spacetime; tipped, disorderly cones depict curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Cone tilt in a drawing depends on the coordinates chosen; locally every cone can be straightened, and curvature is really the impossibility of doing so everywhere at once.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Light-cone field viewer with a 'sober up here' click that straightens cones locally but not globally.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Newton's gravity as clockwork with no visible gear wheels
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Seventeenth-century mechanical taste is invoked to explain why an influence with no mechanism felt unsatisfying.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: GR does not supply a mechanical mechanism either; it replaces the question with geometry.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A field as a machine that takes a position and returns an amplitude
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives an input-output picture of scalar, vector and tensor fields, and later of the metric field returning a local distance rule.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Hides the requirement that the output transform correctly under coordinate changes.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Hover probe over a spacetime map: the tooltip displays the local value of a scalar, a vector arrow or a metric matrix.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Rolling a ball uphill and letting it roll back
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Energy spent lifting equals energy returned, so a potential exists.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Friction in real rolling obscures the idealization.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Initially parallel lines that meet or spread
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Failure of Euclid's parallel postulate is the test for curvature, and its physical version is relative drift of free test particles.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Needs the notion of 'straight' lines (geodesics) on a curved space, which comes later.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two ants walking straight on plane, sphere and saddle surfaces, with their separation plotted versus distance travelled.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Gravity as electrostatics with the sign flipped
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gauss's law and Poisson's equation are shown to have identical structure, with mass for charge and -4 pi G for 1/epsilon_0.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Mass has one sign so gravity always attracts; and GR gravity is nonlinear and tensorial, unlike Maxwell theory.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Once G is measured in a lab, the Earth's mass follows from surface gravity, so a tabletop balance effectively weighs the planet.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Uses the shell theorem and ignores Earth's rotation and oblateness.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: General relativity is only for specialists because its core ideas are intrinsically obscure.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The principles are simple; the historic barrier was unfamiliar geometry, which the book teaches first.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Reputation, heavy tensor notation, and the story that Einstein himself needed a decade and a mathematician friend.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: There is an absolute state of rest against which motion is measured in Newtonian physics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The principle of relativity makes all inertial frames equivalent, so motion is always relative to a chosen frame.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday life treats the ground as 'at rest'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any acceleration of your frame makes simple physics impossible.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Constant acceleration acts like an extra uniform gravitational field and can be compensated; only time-varying acceleration causes trouble.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Standard teaching labels all accelerated frames 'non-inertial' and thus problematic.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'Special' relativity is called special because it is especially important or advanced.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is special in the sense of restricted: inertial frames only, no gravity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravity is a force that travels through space from one mass to another.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In GR gravity is the curvature of spacetime produced by matter; free bodies simply follow that geometry.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian force language and school physics.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Newtonian gravity is essentially perfect and needs no replacement.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Mercury's unexplained 43 arcsec per century precession, and conceptual problems with action at a distance, required GR.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian gravity works superbly for almost all solar-system phenomena.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Relativistic effects only matter for speeds near c or fields where |Phi| is close to c^2.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: GPS clocks and Mercury's orbit show measurable GR effects in weak fields at low speeds, because of precision or accumulation over time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The criterion |Phi| ~ c^2 is presented as the breakdown scale.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Objects dense enough to trap light cannot exist since stars resemble the Sun in density.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Quantum-mechanically supported compact objects such as neutron stars reach nuclear densities; black holes need not be huge.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Nineteenth-century evidence came from solar-system bodies within a factor five of water's density.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The bold G and T in G = 8 pi T are Newton's constant and temperature.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are the Einstein tensor and the energy-momentum tensor; Newton's constant is hidden by setting it to 1.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Setting G = c = 1 changes the physics or loses information.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is only a choice of units; constants can always be restored uniquely by dimensional analysis.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Equations visibly lose factors and quantities like mass acquire units of length.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Tipped light cones in a diagram prove spacetime is curved.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Cone tilt can be produced in flat spacetime by odd coordinates and removed locally in curved spacetime; curvature is the impossibility of aligning all cones at once, equivalently tidal relative acceleration.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Fig. 3 pairs tilted cones directly with the word 'curved'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Any gravitational field, even a uniform one, makes neighbouring free particles move relative to each other.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A uniform field accelerates both equally; only field gradients (tides) produce relative motion, which is what curvature measures.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter states that relative motion of parallel test particles signals a gravitational field without saying 'non-uniform'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Only mass (or energy density) is the source of gravity in GR.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The full energy-momentum tensor, including pressure, momentum density and stresses, sources curvature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word equation lists only 'energy density of matter fields' and the Newtonian analogue has only rho.

thought_experiments.name: The juggler in four frames
thought_experiments.setup: A juggler performs on a fixed floor, on a train at steady speed, on a steadily accelerating train and on a jerking train.
thought_experiments.lesson: Inertial frames are equivalent; steady acceleration mimics gravity; changing acceleration breaks simple laws.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Juggling lab with frame modes and a ground/platform view toggle.

thought_experiments.name: Which train is moving?
thought_experiments.setup: Seated in a train at a platform, you see the adjacent train start to move.
thought_experiments.lesson: Uniform relative motion is undetectable without an external reference.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Two-window train view with the platform hidden until the learner commits to an answer.

thought_experiments.name: A crowd of observers each carrying a light cone
thought_experiments.setup: Fill spacetime with many observers and draw each one's light cone.
thought_experiments.lesson: If all cones are identically aligned, spacetime is flat; disordered cones represent curvature and gravity.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Light-cone field viewer driven by selectable metrics.

thought_experiments.name: Two test particles launched in parallel
thought_experiments.setup: Release two small neutral particles side by side with equal velocities along parallel paths.
thought_experiments.lesson: Any change in their separation reveals gravity as curvature, the physical form of the parallel-postulate test.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drop two balls toward a planet and watch them converge as they fall radially inward; switch to a uniform field to see no convergence.

thought_experiments.name: How big must a star be to trap light?
thought_experiments.setup: Take a body of fixed density and grow its radius until Newtonian escape speed hits c.
thought_experiments.lesson: Ordinary densities need radii beyond an AU, so dark stars seemed impossible until compact objects were understood.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Slider for density (water to nuclear) showing the critical radius compared with Earth's orbit and a neutron star.

thought_experiments.name: When does potential energy rival rest energy?
thought_experiments.setup: Compare m|Phi| with mc^2 for various bodies.
thought_experiments.lesson: |Phi|/c^2 near one signals strong gravity, but precision and accumulated effects reveal GR far earlier.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Log-scale ladder of |Phi|/c^2 from Earth (7e-10) through Sun (2e-6), white dwarf and neutron star (0.2) to a black-hole horizon (0.5).

historical_notes.event: Accepted the principle that physical laws do not distinguish between uniformly moving frames.
historical_notes.significance: Relativity predates Einstein; his innovation was adding the light-speed postulate.

historical_notes.event: Added the invariance of light speed to the principle of relativity, founding special relativity.
historical_notes.significance: First step toward the geometric picture of spacetime.

historical_notes.event: Principia presents universal gravitation, unifying the fall of an apple with the Moon's orbit.
historical_notes.significance: Launched the first quantitative theory of gravity, later the weak-field limit of GR. (The book dates it 1686, when it was presented; publication was 1687.)

historical_notes.event: In the preface to the Opticks, Newton declined to treat gravity as an essential property of matter because he did not know its cause.
historical_notes.significance: Shows Newton recognized the missing mechanism that GR later addresses.

historical_notes.event: Torsion-balance measurement of the attraction between lead spheres, determining G and 'weighing the world'.
historical_notes.significance: Made absolute masses of Earth and Sun calculable.

historical_notes.event: Wrote that the theory of gravitation was essentially perfect, citing Lagrange and Laplace on solar-system stability (chapter epigraph).
historical_notes.significance: Used ironically: the Mercury discrepancy proved significant.

historical_notes.event: Grossmann helped Einstein learn the geometry needed for GR; Einstein then worked roughly a further decade to complete the theory.
historical_notes.significance: Explains why mathematical preparation is front-loaded in the book.

historical_notes.event: Developed modern geometric techniques (differential forms, moving frames) that reshaped how GR is presented.
Could not prove the parallel postulate; eighteenth- and nineteenth-century geometers built consistent geometries without it.
historical_notes.significance: Supplies the operational definition of curvature used throughout the book.

historical_notes.event: Greek astronomers estimated the Earth-Sun distance from the angle between the Sun and a half-Moon; seventeenth-century and later transit-of-Venus observations refined it.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates how astronomical scale was bootstrapped geometrically. (The book does not name Aristarchus.)

historical_notes.event: Coined the two-line summary that spacetime governs motion of matter and matter governs curvature of spacetime.
historical_notes.significance: The book's slogan for the geometric view of gravity.

applications_and_observations.topic: Mass and density of the Earth
applications_and_observations.details: Surface gravity, Earth's radius and Cavendish's G give the Earth's mass and mean density.

applications_and_observations.topic: Mass and density of the Sun
applications_and_observations.details: Continuing inside the Example 0.3 box: circular-orbit balance with one AU and one year gives the Sun's mass, and its radius gives a density just above water's. A shaded margin data box collects the Earth and Sun figures.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: AU = 1.496e11 m; M_sun = 1.99e30 kg; R_sun = 6.96e8 m; density 1.4e3 kg m^-3; M_sun/M_earth = 3.33e5; R_sun/R_earth = 1.09e2.

applications_and_observations.topic: Half-Moon method for the astronomical unit
applications_and_observations.details: At exact half-Moon the Sun-Moon-Earth angle is a right angle; measuring the Moon-Sun angle from Earth gives the ratio of distances (Fig. 6).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Angle 89.853 degrees; Earth-Moon distance 0.00257 AU (own check: cos 89.853 deg = 0.00257).

applications_and_observations.details: Radius at which escape speed equals c for a given density; for solar-system densities it exceeds an AU, so black holes seemed implausible.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: R = c/sqrt(8 pi G rho). Own estimates: about 1.5 AU for water density, about 0.66 AU for Earth's density.

applications_and_observations.details: Clocks at different heights in Earth's field tick at measurably different rates, which satellite navigation must correct.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate: Earth-surface |Phi|/c^2 is about 7e-10; the net relativistic GPS clock correction is about 38 microseconds per day (external figure, not in the chapter).

applications_and_observations.details: Mercury's orbit precesses by about 575 arcsec per century; Newtonian planetary perturbations account for about 532; the remaining 43 was explained by GR.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Orbital speed 47 km/s (below 0.0002c); 575, 532 and 43 arcsec per century. Own check: 6 pi GM/(c^2 a (1-e^2)) per orbit gives 43 arcsec per century.

applications_and_observations.topic: Surface gravity and escape speed of Earth, Sun and a neutron star (Exercise 0.2)
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimates (consistent with GA Appendix E): Earth 9.8 m s^-2, 11.2 km/s; Sun 274 m s^-2, 618 km/s; 1.4 M_sun, 10 km neutron star 1.9e12 m s^-2, 1.9e8 m/s (0.64c), |Phi|/c^2 about 0.21.

applications_and_observations.topic: Tidal stretching of a human near black holes (Exercise 0.3)
applications_and_observations.details: Head-to-foot tidal acceleration difference 2GMh/r^3 for h = 1.8 m.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimates: Earth surface 5.5e-6 m s^-2; at r_s = 8.9 km of a 3 M_sun hole about 2e9 m s^-2 (lethal); at r_s = 3.0e9 m of a 1e6 M_sun hole about 0.019 m s^-2 (harmless). Tidal acceleration at the horizon scales as 1/M^2.

Circle-plus denotes the Earth and circle-dot the Sun (M_earth, R_sun, etc.); R_ES is the Earth-Sun distance.

notable.summary: Use energy conservation to get the Newtonian escape speed from a star, express it via the potential, and find the radius where it equals c.
notable.why_notable: Produces 2GM/c^2 by a Newtonian coincidence, a hook for Part IV and a caution that the derivation is not the GR one.

notable.summary: Compute surface gravity and escape speed for the Earth, the Sun and a 1.4 solar-mass neutron star of 10 km radius.
notable.why_notable: Escape speed rises from about 4e-5 c (Earth) through about 0.002c (Sun) to about 0.64c (neutron star), which makes the need for GR vivid.

notable.summary: Estimate the head-to-foot tidal force on a 1.8 m person on Earth and at the horizon radius of a 3 solar-mass and of a million solar-mass black hole.
notable.why_notable: Counter-intuitive result that tides at the horizon are gentler for bigger black holes; previews curvature as tidal effect (GA ch11). Note that the person's mass must be assumed or the answer given per unit mass.

exercises.solutions: Appendix E (appE) gives short answers to all three. Its 0.2 answers agree with the own estimates recorded here (Earth 11.2 km/s, about 4e-5 c; Sun 6.2e5 m/s; neutron star 1.9e8 m/s, about 0.64c). For 0.3 it quotes fractional differences |dF|/|F| = 2h/r: about 0.6 ppm on Earth and about 4e-4 at the 3-solar-mass horizon (both consistent), but about 4e-10 for the million-solar-mass hole, where 2h/r_s = 3.6 m / 2.95e9 m gives about 1.2e-9 (own check). It also notes that tidal force at the horizon scales as M^-2.

difficulty.notes: Mostly verbal survey plus standard first-year Newtonian gravity. The one mathematically dense passage is the flux/divergence-theorem/delta-function route to Poisson's equation, which moves quickly and hides a step (from eqn 9 to eqn 12). Relativistic ideas (covariance, light cones, metric field, curvature) are named with pictures but no formulas, so the reader gains vocabulary rather than working knowledge; some glosses are loose (classical field theory, energy density as the sole source).
